title: Signals: Angular's Reactivity
summary: Values that know when they change — and update the screen for you.
heading: Signals: Angular's Reactivity

blocks.text: A signal is a value that knows when it changes. When you update a signal, anything that depends on it — other values, and the screen — updates automatically. You no longer have to manually find an element and change it like we did with the DOM; Angular tracks the connections for you.

blocks.caption: Change the signal, and everything that depends on it updates by itself.

blocks.text: Create a signal with signal(startValue). To read it, you call it like a function with (). To change it, use set (a new value) or update (based on the old value).

blocks.label: signal

blocks.text: In a template you read it the same way: {{ count() }}. When count changes, that spot on the screen refreshes on its own.

Try the reactive idea live — click the button and the number on screen updates by itself. (The mini-preview uses a plain property; in a real app this would be a signal, but the auto-updating behaviour is the same.)
A computed signal is built from other signals. You never set it directly — it recalculates itself whenever the signals it reads change.

blocks.label: computed

blocks.text: An effect runs a piece of code whenever the signals it uses change. It's for side effects — things like saving to storage or logging — not for calculating values.

blocks.label: effect

blocks.text: This very app uses signals — the light/dark theme and the current chapter are stored as signals, and the page reacts when they change.

items: A signal is a value that tracks its own changes.
computed builds a value from other signals and refreshes itself.
effect runs code when the signals it uses change.
This is how modern Angular keeps the screen in sync with your data.
